newsitem.title: USA: Clinton pays tribute to Jackie Robinson.
newsitem.headline: Clinton pays tribute to Jackie Robinson.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton led baseball fans on Tuesday night in observing the 50th anniversary of the day Jackie Robinson, a brilliant black athlete, shattered the sport's colour barrier.

Two days after Tiger Woods became the first black to win the Masters golf tournament, Robinson's breakthrough was remembered in a ceremony at Shea Stadium after the fifth inning of the game between the New York Mets and the Los Angeles Dodgers, who were the Brooklyn Dodgers when Robinson played for them.

Standing at home plate on a chilly night with Robinson's widow Rachel and acting baseball commissioner Bud Selig, Clinton told a sellout crowd that Robinson's example "proved that America is a better, stronger, richer country when we all work together and give everyone a chance."

Clinton was less than a year old when Robinson took the field with the Dodgers in a season-opening game against the Boston Braves on April 15, 1947, becoming the first black American to integrate Major League Baseball in modern times.

Clinton said Robinson paved the way for many advances in race relations in the United States but that if he were still alive, he would say that "We can do better." Robinson died of a heart attack at age 53 in 1972.

"We have achieved equality on the playing field, but we need to establish equality in the boardrooms of baseball and throughout corporate America," said Clinton, standing on crutches as he continued his recovery from knee surgery.

"Even as we celebrate his brilliant successor, Tiger Woods' victory in the Masters, we need even more of our young people from all walks of life to get their master's degrees and help to make more of their lives in this country," he said.
Clinton had invited Woods to join him at Shea Stadium to celebrate Robinson's historic accomplishment, but the White House said the 21-year-old golf phenomenon politely declined.
"He (Woods) felt very strongly that he needed some time out of the limelight, and tonight would very much have been in the limelight, obviously," White House spokesman Barry Toiv said.
Toiv said the president did not feel Woods was snubbing him. "Not at all," he said. "Everyone here understood perfectly."

Unlike Woods, who has known mostly adulation, Robinson endured a stream of insults and physical threats from racist fans and players, including some of his own teammates, and went on to such a brilliant career he won over many of his opponents.
He paved the way for a long line of black players who became major stars over the next 50 years.

Selig announced that Major League Baseball would retire Robinson's number 42 permanently. Players who currently wear it may continue for the rest of their career but no club will ever issue uniforms with that number again, he said.
In an ESPN television interview during the game, Clinton said he hoped the Robinson observance would help baseball rebound after losing some fans from its strike two years ago.

"This night will capture the attention of America and make everybody forget about some of the things they didn't like that happened the last two years and make people fall in love iwth baseball again, I hope," he said.
His trip to New York was his first domestic outing since he underwent surgery on March 14 to repair a right knee tendon torn when he stumbled at the Florida home of golf pro Greg Norman.
